title: Course final: .NET inside out
sub: From CIL to the hot path — test yourself
cards/0/q: The path of a hot method from source to the best machine code in .NET 8
cards/0/items/0: The C# compiler turns the method into CIL
cards/0/items/1: CIL and metadata go into the assembly
cards/0/items/2: First call: the stub calls the JIT and Tier 0 comes out
cards/0/items/3: An instrumented version collects the profile
cards/0/items/4: A background thread builds Tier 1 using the profile
cards/0/explain: The whole course in one chain: the compiler, the assembly, the JIT on demand, and then the runtime refines hot code from a live profile.
cards/1/q: A command-line tool runs thousands of times a day in CI and works for a fraction of a second. No reflection, no plugins. What gives the biggest win?
cards/1/options/0: Native AOT: no JIT and no CIL loading at startup
cards/1/options/1: Dynamic PGO: the profile will speed up hot methods
cards/1/explain: The program lives so briefly that almost nothing reaches Tier 1: all the time is startup. Native AOT removes the JIT entirely, and its restrictions do not get in the way here.
cards/1/wrong/1: PGO pays off over long runs. In a fraction of a second the profile has no time to be collected, let alone used.
cards/1/wrong/3: Without tiers every method is compiled fully optimized right away — startup only gets slower.
cards/2/q: What is true about code after warmup? Select all.
cards/2/options/0: A static readonly bool can become a constant in Tier 1, and the branch disappears
cards/2/options/1: AggressiveInlining lets you inline a virtual call with an unknown type
cards/2/options/2: sealed helps the JIT call a method directly
cards/2/options/4: Guarded devirtualization keeps a fallback virtual call
cards/2/explain: AggressiveInlining only lifts the size limit: it cannot tell whose body to insert when the type is unknown. Tier 0 inlines nothing.
cards/3/q: Which line allocates a heap object for a boxed int?
cards/3/explain: Assigning a value type to object is boxing: an object with a header and a type pointer appears on the heap. Unboxing with (int)o copies the value back, and int to long is an ordinary widening with no heap involved.
cards/4/q: Match the course concept to what it means
cards/5/q: A method was timed with a Stopwatch: one call right after the program started. What was actually measured?
cards/5/options/0: JIT time and slow Tier 0 code, not the steady-state speed
cards/5/options/1: The peak speed of the method after warmup
cards/5/options/3: The speed of code from a ReadyToRun image
cards/5/explain: The first call goes through the stub and the JIT, and the resulting code is Tier 0 without inlining. Only warmup and many iterations show the steady-state speed — which is what BenchmarkDotNet does.
cards/6/q: Add an allocations column and a comparison against the reference
cards/6/explain: [MemoryDiagnoser] adds Allocated and Gen0, Baseline = true adds a Ratio column relative to Old. Both methods return their result, so the JIT will not throw the computation away.
cards/7/q: What is missing from an app built with Native AOT? Select all.
cards/7/options/3: Loading new assemblies on the fly
cards/7/explain: The garbage collector and the type system are part of the small Native AOT runtime — memory is still managed and GetType works. There is no JIT, and so no tiers, no PGO and no loading of new code.
cards/8/q: A program uses List<int>, List<long>, List<string> and List<object>. How many distinct machine-code versions of the Add method will the JIT produce?
cards/8/explain: Every value type T gets its own copy: int and long. All reference T share one piece of code — a reference is always pointer-sized. Three in total.
cards/8/wrong/1: string and object are reference types; they share code.
cards/8/wrong/2: int and long differ in size and the code handles them differently — the copies are separate.
